source_read: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/DiCastelnuovo_2006_AlcoholDosingTotalMortalityMA.pdf (reprint from the publisher's site), printed pp. 2437-2445 (all pages, text layer; Tables 1-3 and Figures 1-4 checked on rendered pp. 2438-2443; Table 1 per-study counts summed: 1,015,835 subjects and 94,533 deaths, as printed).

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of strength: 'no longer significant' is the source's own definition of its reversion point (99% level), and the source gives no dose at which mortality becomes significantly higher. No amount is worded as advice; the authors' own advice (p. 2444) is rightly not repeated.
claims.note: Numbers match Table 2: reversion point 42 g/d for all 56 curves, 18 g/d in women and 38 g/d in men. Two problems for this source. (1) The reference group is not named for the 2006 estimate: the sentence reads as 'compared with non-drinkers', but the 2006 curves were against each study's lowest-intake category, which was no intake with former drinkers excluded in 30 of 56 curves, self-declared non-drinkers (former drinkers not excluded) in 12 and occasional drinkers in 14. (2) The 42 g figure is for all 56 curves, including 8 unadjusted ones (reversion 68 g); the sex-specific 18 and 38 g come from the 48 curves adjusted at least for age, whose combined reversion point is 37 g. Suggested: '42 g a day in all 56 curves (37 g in the 48 adjusted curves: 18 g in women, 38 g in men), against each study's lowest-intake category'. Editors' calculation recomputed from the Table 3 parameters (log RR = b1*sqrt(x) + b2*sqrt(x)*ln x, so RR = 1 at x = exp(-b1/b2)): all 43.9, men 41.4, women 25.2 g/d, i.e. 44, 41 and 25 (same); the age-adjusted curve crosses at 40.6 g/d. All estimates are from a fixed-effect model; the random-effects curve was similar with wider intervals (not printed). The source's warning that under-reporting may distort the apparent threshold for harm (p. 2443) supports the claim's caveat on reported amounts.

anchors.extracted: Reversion point = dose at which the lower total mortality is no longer significant at the 99% level. All 56 curves (1,015,835 subjects, 94,533 deaths): 42 g/d. In the 48 adjusted curves: adjusted at least for age 37 g/d; women (16 curves, 285,490 subjects, 13,448 deaths) 18 g/d; men (32 curves, 622,692, 73,493) 38 g/d. Unadjusted (8 curves) 68 g/d.

log RR = b1*sqrt(x) + b2*sqrt(x)*ln(x). All: b1 -0.1592 (SE 0.0056), b2 0.0421 (0.0014); men -0.1445, 0.0388; women -0.1719, 0.0533; adjusted at least for age -0.1437, 0.0388. Editors' calculation: the curves reach RR 1 at exp(-b1/b2) = 43.9 g/d (all), 41.4 (men), 25.2 (women), 40.6 (age-adjusted).

J-shaped fitted curve: lower mortality up to 42 g/d (about 4 drinks), lowest at 6 g/d (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.80-0.83). Random-effects re-analysis gave a very similar curve with wider intervals (not printed); deviance 879.4 (fixed) vs 154.0 (random), P < .001, indicating heterogeneity.

anchors.locator: Results > Adjusted Studies in Men and Women, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: In the 48 adjusted curves (32 men, 16 women) the sexes differed (P < .001; b2 larger in women): lower mortality up to 3 drinks a day in men and 2 in women (the abstract, p. 2437, says up to 4 in men); maximum reduction 17% (99% CI 15-19%) in men, 18% (13-22%) in women.
Reference category: no alcohol intake with former drinkers excluded in 30 of 56 curves; self-declared non-drinkers in 12 and occasional drinkers in 14, former drinkers excluded from neither.
The authors note that under-reported intake would bias relative risks toward the null and may have distorted the J-curve's shape and the apparent threshold for harm.

claims.overstatement: None in strength: the claim avoids the authors' causal wording (protection, net beneficial effect) and their advice that people drinking low to moderate amounts be encouraged to continue (p. 2444). The 0.81 (0.80 to 0.83) is a fixed-effect estimate whose narrow interval does not reflect the between-study heterogeneity the authors report (p. 2440); the magnitude says fixed-effect, the statement does not. '6 g a day, about half a drink' follows the source's own wording (drink sizes as each study defined them, 10 g where undefined). No amount reads as advice.
claims.note: All 2006 figures match: 34 studies, 56 curves, 1,015,835 subjects, 94,533 deaths (Table 1 rows and the Table 2 subgroup sums recomputed: same); lowest RR 0.81 (95% CI 0.80-0.83) at 6 g/d, lower up to 42 g/d; adjusted at least for age 17% (99% CI 15-18) at 6 g, to 37 g; with light and/or former drinkers in the reference 23% (20-26) at 8 g, to 52 g (21 curves, 247,194 subjects, 23,937 deaths); without them 16% (14-18) at 5 g, to 30 g (27 curves, 660,988, 63,004), difference P < .001; same 34 curves 19% (17-21) unadjusted against 16% (14-18) adjusted. Minima recomputed from the printed parameters agree (5.9 g/d, RR 0.81; 8.3 g, 22.5%; 4.6 g, 16.0%). The part not supported for this source is the comparison-group description: 'non-drinkers ... who in most studies included people who had stopped drinking or drank occasionally' does not fit the 2006 set as its authors coded it, where 30 of 56 curves used no intake with former drinkers excluded (12 non-drinkers including former drinkers, 14 occasional drinkers; in the 48 adjusted curves 21 with and 27 without light or former drinkers). The 2006 coding is the authors' and less strict than the later Stockwell group's (it does not say whether lifetime occasional drinking was excluded), so the claim could keep its general statement but should give the 2006 reference as in its magnitude: each study's lowest-intake category, non-drinkers excluding former drinkers in 30 of 56 curves and occasional drinkers in 14. The subgroup that 'left out former and light drinkers' is described inconsistently by the source (Table 2: without light and/or former drinkers; Results: no intake with former drinkers excluded; Figure 4A: no drinkers in the reference group; Comment: excluded either ex-drinkers or very light drinkers), so 'former and light' may be stricter than every study in it was; its 'cohorts' are 27 and 21 curves. RRs only, no absolute rates (editors' observation confirmed).

anchors.extracted: 34 studies gave 56 curves (37 men, 19 women), 1,015,835 subjects and 94,533 deaths; 28 curves European, 17 American, 11 other. Lowest mortality at 6 g/d, about half a drink a day, RR 0.81 (95% CI 0.80-0.83); lower mortality up to 42 g/d. Fixed-effect weighting; random-effects curve similar with wider intervals; deviance 879.4 vs 154.0 (P < .001).

anchors.locator: Table 2, rows All, Level of adjustment and Type of reference group
anchors.extracted: All 56 curves: maximum reduction 19% (95% CI 17-20) at 6 g/d, reversion 42 g/d. Unadjusted (8 curves): 36% (21-40) at 10 g, 68 g. Adjusted at least for age (48; 908,182 subjects, 86,941 deaths): 17% (99% CI 15-18) at 6 g, 37 g. Reference with light and/or former drinkers (21 curves; 247,194; 23,937): 23% (20-26) at 8 g, 52 g. Without (27; 660,988; 63,004): 16% (14-18) at 5 g, 30 g.

anchors.locator: Results > All Studies, 1st paragraph (reference category, p. 2439); Methods > Search Strategy and Data Extraction, 1st paragraph (begins p. 2437; exclusion list on p. 2438)
anchors.extracted: Reference: no alcohol intake with former drinkers excluded in 30 curves; self-declared non-drinkers in 12 and occasional drinkers in 14, former drinkers excluded from neither. Studies were excluded if the reference was not the lowest-intake category (4 publications).

Maximum reduction fell from 36% in unadjusted to 17% in adjusted curves; in the 34 curves with both, 19% (99% CI 17-21) unadjusted against 16% (14-18) adjusted. Adjustment for social status and diet did not change results.

anchors.locator: Results > Other Subgroup Analyses, 1st paragraph (with Figure 4A, p. 2443, and Table 3, type of reference group, p. 2440)
anchors.extracted: Curves whose reference was no intake with former drinkers excluded showed a significantly smaller reduction (P < .001); Figure 4A labels the two groups no drinkers in the reference (27 curves) and occasional and former drinkers in the reference (21).

The authors acknowledge that non-drinker groups may include people who stopped because of illness; restricting to studies that excluded either ex-drinkers or very light drinkers gave a smaller but still significant reduction.

The authors argue that residual confounding is very unlikely to change the picture and that the true maximum reduction would still exceed 10%, and conclude that low-to-moderate intake may confer a net survival benefit: a causal reading the design cannot test, on one side of the dispute the claim describes.

key_findings.correction: Numbers confirmed, but 'further adjustment for social status and diet did not change the results' repeats the text (p. 2440) against Table 3 (p. 2440), whose difference column gives P < .001 for curves adjusted for social status (28) against the other adjusted curves (20) and P = .03 for social status plus diet (10) against social status only. The curves differed in shape (reversion points 37, 46 and 30 g/d) while maximum protection was similar (17%, 18%, 18%). Read: 'maximum protection was similar with further adjustment, but the curves differed (P < .001; P = .03)'.

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed from Table 3: small studies 14.3% at 5.2 g/d, large 16.9% at 5.5 g/d; women's minimum at 3.4 g/d, social-status curves at 7.4 g/d.

Recomputed: adjusted curves by region (Table 2) plus the 8 unadjusted curves, all from European studies (Table 1, adjustment NR), give 27 European, 16 US, 13 other; Table 1 code 3 gives 27 curves adjusted for social class.
Recomputed: large-study b1 z = 2.20 (two-sided P = .028); women 'other countries' b2 z = 1.98, two-sided .048, one-sided .024; b1 z = 2.28, two-sided .023, one-sided .011 (printed .01).

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2, critically low: items 2, 4, 7, 11 and 15 are 'no' on what the article shows (no protocol; PubMed only; exclusions as counts; fixed-effect intervals despite deviance 879.4 vs 154.0; publication bias argued, not tested). Item 9 'partial yes' is generous but defensible (studies grouped by adjustment level and reference-group composition).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: causal and advisory wording (protection, net benefit, encouragement to continue) from fixed-effect pooling of observational cohorts; the reference-group result, which moves the reversion point from 52 to 30 g/d, is absent from the abstract and conclusion. The card's recomputed curve values (key finding 15) are correct.

missed: Reporting issue: text against Table 3 (p. 2440). The Results say adjustment for social status and dietary markers did not affect the results, but Table 3 reports significant differences (P < .001 for social status; P = .03 for diet). Table 3's footnote ‡ also gives n = 8 for curves adjusted for social status but not diet, where 28 - 10 = 18 (editors' arithmetic).

Weight of one study: Boffetta and Garfinkel (1990; men only, adjusted for age and smoking only) contributes 239,462 of 1,015,835 participants (24%) and 37,079 of 94,533 deaths (39%) (Table 1, p. 2438; editors' arithmetic). Under fixed-effect inverse-variance weighting it probably carries a large share of the pooled curve; weights are not reported and no analysis without it is given.
Non-independent curves: Renaud et al. (1999) contributes separate wine and beer curves from the same cohort of men, counted among the '56 independent curves' (p. 2438).
